extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating patentability under 35 U.S.C. §103 (obviousness), including analogous art, claim comparison to prior art, level of ordinary skill, prima facie burdens, and enumerated rationales for finding obviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogous art (field of endeavor / same problem / structural similarity)
rubrics_metrics.description: A reference is analogous art if it is within the field of the inventor's endeavor or if it is reasonably pertinent to the particular problem the inventor was trying to solve; structural similarity or common problems across fields can render art analogous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the field-of-endeavor test and the problem-solved test. Consider whether a person of ordinary skill would look to the other art for solutions (examples: toothbrush references to a hair brush claim; fastener/hinge art to pen holding means; clutch art to braking materials). Use case law examples from mechanical, electrical, and design arts to determine analogousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider the claimed invention 'as a whole'
rubrics_metrics.description: In determining differences between prior art and claims under 35 U.S.C. 103, the claimed invention must be considered as an integrated whole, not by focusing solely on isolated differences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret claim language and view both the invention and referenced art as wholes. Do not improperly limit analysis to a single structural difference if the overall invention yields a new result or insight (see Stratoflex, Schenck examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not distill an invention to a 'gist' or 'thrust'
rubrics_metrics.description: Reducing an invention to a broad gist or single advantage ignores statutory requirement to analyze the invention as a whole and may lead to improper obviousness findings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respect all express claim limitations; avoid treating the advantage or one characteristic as the entire invention (cases: W.L. Gore, Bausch & Lomb).

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery of source/cause of a problem as part of 'as a whole' inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: Discovery of the underlying cause of a problem can be part of the invention-as-a-whole analysis and may support patentability, but discovery alone does not guarantee patentability if the solution would have been obvious from prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the discovery changed the understanding of the art and whether the prior art already contained the same solution for a similar problem (see In re Sponnoble and In re Wiseman examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicants alleging discovery must provide substantiating evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant asserting that they discovered the source of a problem must substantiate that allegation with evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence may be affidavits/declarations or a clear and persuasive disclosure in the specification; unsupported counsel statements or unsubstantiated assertions are insufficient (see In re Wiseman, In re Kaslow).

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosed inherent properties are part of the 'as a whole' inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: Properties inherent in the claimed subject matter and disclosed in the specification are considered when delineating the invention as a whole for obviousness analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider inherent properties (e.g., optimized parameters, ratios) disclosed in the specification as part of what must be obvious under 35 U.S.C. 103. Obviousness cannot be based on knowledge of inherency established only after the invention (see In re Antonie, In re Rijckaert and MPEP §2112).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art must be considered in its entirety, including teachings that teach away
rubrics_metrics.description: A prior art reference must be read as a whole, including portions that may discourage or teach away from the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If portions of the prior art would lead away from the claimed invention, that can undermine an obviousness conclusion (W.L. Gore example). Conversely, mere disclosure of alternatives in prior art does not necessarily amount to teaching away (In re Fulton). Evaluate the whole reference and its impact on the motivation to combine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Level of ordinary skill in the art (definition and factors)
rubrics_metrics.description: The person of ordinary skill is a hypothetical person presumed to know the relevant art at the time of invention; determining this level is necessary and affects obviousness analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider factors such as: (A) type of problems encountered; (B) prior art solutions; (C) rapidity of innovations; (D) sophistication of the technology; (E) educational level of active workers. The person is of ordinary creativity, not an automaton (KSR). Use references (even non-prior or not widely disseminated) to show the appropriate skill level when relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specifying a particular level of skill not always necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not always necessary to specifically identify the level of ordinary skill if the prior art of record already reflects an appropriate level.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When facts of record about skill are contained in the prior art itself, a separate explicit finding of skill level may be unnecessary (e.g., Chore-Time Equipment v. Cumberland).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ascertainment of skill level required to maintain objectivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Resolving the level of ordinary skill is essential to keep the obviousness inquiry objective and avoid judging by inventor, judge, or other inappropriate standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners must determine what would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill at the relevant time, not to the inventor or to experts in remote arts (Ryko Mfg. Co.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prima facie obviousness: examiner's initial burden and articulation requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The examiner bears the initial burden of factually supporting any prima facie conclusion of obviousness; an explicit reasoned explanation linking facts to the legal conclusion is required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the examiner fails to produce a prima facie case, the applicant need not submit rebuttal evidence. If a prima facie case is made, the burden shifts to applicant to rebut (e.g., with comparative test data). Examiners must avoid hindsight, step into the shoes of the hypothetical skilled person, and evaluate the record as a whole. Evidence submitted late (after final rejection) may be denied entry; compact prosecution encourages early submission of evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard of proof and final determination
rubrics_metrics.description: The ultimate patentability determination is made on the entire record by a preponderance of the evidence with consideration of persuasiveness of arguments and secondary evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners must provide facts showing the prima facie case is more probable than not; when applicant submits evidence, the examiner must reconsider rejections in light of all evidence (In re Oetiker, In re Piasecki, In re Eli Lilly).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exemplary rationales that may support a conclusion of obviousness (KSR-consistent)
rubrics_metrics.description: Several lines of reasoning may justify a conclusion of obviousness; the examiner must link factual findings to these rationales.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common rationales include: (A) combining prior art elements according to known methods to yield predictable results; (B) simple substitution of one known element for another to obtain predictable results; (C) using known techniques to improve similar devices in the same way; (D) applying a known technique to a known device ready for improvement; (E) 'obvious to try' when choosing from a finite number of identified, predictable solutions with a reasonable expectation of success; (F) variations prompted by known work in one field leading to predictable variations in another; (G) some teaching, suggestion, or motivation in the prior art to modify or combine references. The list is not exhaustive; any rationale used must provide a link between factual findings and the legal conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirements for using the 'combine prior art elements' rationale
rubrics_metrics.description: To reject under the rationale that prior art elements could be combined by known methods to yield predictable results, specific factual findings are required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Office personnel must articulate: (1) prior art included each claimed element (not necessarily in one reference); (2) one of ordinary skill could have combined the elements by known methods and each element would perform the same function; (3) one of ordinary skill would have recognized the combination's results as predictable; and (4) any additional Graham-fact findings necessary in the particular case. If any of these findings cannot be made, this rationale cannot support obviousness.
